result:
I tested 7 properties on `eml_parser.parser` and found 2 real bugs; the other 5 properties passed. Everything is in `runs/eml-parser_v2_r4/work/`.

### Bug 1 — Received headers take quadratic time (High, a denial-of-service)
`parse_email` runs `email_regex.findall` over each whole `Received:` line (`parser.py:404`), and there is no length limit. A long run of characters that could start an e-mail address, with no `@domain` after it, makes the regex try again from every position. So the time grows with the square of the header length:

| Header size | Parse time |
|---|---|
| 32 KB | 1.16 s |
| 64 KB | 4.3 s |
| 128 KB | 17.2 s |
| 1 MB | about 18 min (extrapolated) |

The sender writes these headers, so anyone can send a mail that ties up a service parsing untrusted e-mail. The code already cuts the body into slices because of this exact problem (comment at `parser.py:468`), but headers get no such protection. The report proposes a lookbehind fix that brings 128 KB down to 0.001 s. It reports one fewer match in a rare case (a match that starts right where the previous one ended), so I also give a second option: slice the Received lines the same way as the body.
→ `bug_report_eml_parser_parser_2026-10-28_19-47_l68k.md`

### Bug 2 — `ignore_bad_start=True` mangles the e-mail (Medium, wrong results)
Two separate defects in `decode_email_bytes` (`parser.py:227-237`):
- `_eml_file += line` drops the newline after every line, so the whole message becomes one `From:` header. `From: a@b.com\nTo: c@d.com…` parses as `from='a@b.comto'`, `to=[]`.
- `b':' not in eml_file.split(b'\n', 1)` checks whether `b':'` is an item in a list, not whether the first line contains a colon. It is almost always true, so even a well-formed e-mail gets mangled. The test failed on every input.

The report includes a short patch for both.
→ `bug_report_eml_parser_parser_2026-10-28_19-47_gp1g.md`

### Properties that passed
- `get_hash` gives the same result as `hashlib`.
- `get_valid_domain_or_ip` returns IPv4/IPv6 addresses (bare or `x@[ip]`) in their standard string form.
- `headeremail2list` returns the To addresses lowercased and in order.
- `decode_email_bytes` raised no exception on 500 random header/body inputs.
- `string_sliding_window_loop` returned slices that together cover the whole body.

I did not construct an input that should make each of these fail, so I haven't confirmed the tests could have caught a bug. The no-crash and sliding-window tests are the weakest: the sliding-window test finds where each slice sits by searching the body text, which is approximate.

The claims and their evidence are in `claims.md`, and the tests are in `test_parser.py`.
